glossary.definition: A fraudulent attempt to obtain sensitive information (such as usernames, passwords, or credit card details) by disguising oneself as a trustworthy entity in electronic communications.
glossary.analogy: Like a fisherman casting bait — the attacker sends out many fake messages hoping someone will 'bite' and hand over their details.
examples: Fake bank emails asking you to verify your account
SMS messages claiming your package is delayed with a suspicious link

glossary.definition: A targeted phishing attack directed at a specific individual or organisation, often using personalised information to appear more convincing.
glossary.analogy: Unlike regular phishing (casting a wide net), spear phishing is like a sniper — the attacker researches you specifically to craft a convincing fake.
examples: Email appearing to come from your CEO asking for an urgent wire transfer
Message referencing your recent purchase to seem legitimate

glossary.definition: Phishing conducted via SMS text messages. The attacker sends fake texts to trick victims into clicking malicious links or revealing personal information.
glossary.analogy: The same trick as email phishing, but through your text messages.
examples: 'Your bank account has been suspended — verify now' texts
Fake delivery notification SMS with a link

glossary.definition: Malicious software that encrypts a victim's files and demands payment (a ransom) in exchange for the decryption key to restore access.
glossary.analogy: Like a digital kidnapping — criminals lock up your files and demand money to release them.
examples: WannaCry attack (2017) that paralysed the NHS

glossary.definition: Short for 'malicious software' — any software intentionally designed to cause disruption, damage, or gain unauthorised access to a computer system.
glossary.analogy: Like a disease for your computer — it can make your device sick, slow it down, steal information, or even hand control to an attacker.

glossary.definition: A security method that requires two different forms of identity verification before granting access — typically something you know (password) and something you have (phone).
glossary.analogy: Like a bank vault with two keys — you need both to open it. Even if a thief steals one key, they still can't get in without the second.
examples: Entering a password, then a code sent to your phone
Password + authenticator app code (e.g., Google Authenticator)

glossary.definition: A security system that requires users to verify their identity using two or more independent factors before gaining access.
glossary.analogy: Like a three-lock door — each lock is a different type of key.

glossary.definition: Psychological manipulation of people into performing actions or divulging confidential information. It exploits human psychology rather than technical vulnerabilities.
glossary.analogy: Like a con artist — instead of picking a lock, they convince someone to open the door for them.
examples: Pretending to be IT support to get your password
Creating urgency to make someone act without thinking

glossary.definition: A technology that creates an encrypted, secure tunnel for your internet connection, hiding your IP address and protecting your data from eavesdroppers.
glossary.analogy: Like sending your internet traffic through a private, armoured tunnel instead of an open road — no one can see what's inside.
examples: Using a VPN on public Wi-Fi at a coffee shop
Accessing company resources securely from home

glossary.definition: An incident where confidential or protected information is accessed, disclosed, or stolen without authorisation.
glossary.analogy: Like a thief breaking into a filing cabinet and stealing copies of everyone's personal records.
examples: LinkedIn breach exposing 700 million users' data (2021)

glossary.definition: A software application that generates, stores, and retrieves complex passwords for you, protected behind a single master password.
glossary.analogy: Like a secure keychain that holds all your keys — you only need to remember one master key to access the rest.

glossary.definition: A network security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predefined security rules.
glossary.analogy: Like a security guard at a building entrance — it checks everyone coming in and going out against an allowed list.

glossary.definition: The process of converting data into an unreadable format (ciphertext) using an algorithm and key, so only authorised parties with the correct key can read it.
glossary.analogy: Like writing a message in a secret code — only someone with the codebook can understand it.

glossary.definition: A software security flaw that is unknown to the vendor and for which no patch yet exists. Attackers can exploit it before developers have a chance to fix it.
glossary.analogy: Like finding a secret passage into a bank vault that even the bank designers didn't know existed.

glossary.definition: The fraudulent acquisition and use of a person's private identifying information, usually for financial gain.
glossary.analogy: Someone stealing your name, address, and ID number to pretend to be you — opening bank accounts, taking loans, or committing crimes in your name.
examples: Using stolen SSN to file false tax returns
Opening credit cards with a victim's personal details

glossary.definition: Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure — the secure version of HTTP that encrypts data between your browser and a website using TLS/SSL.
glossary.analogy: HTTP is like sending a postcard anyone can read; HTTPS is like sending a sealed, tamper-proof envelope.

glossary.definition: Malware disguised as legitimate software. Once installed, it can give attackers remote access, steal data, or install additional malware.
glossary.analogy: Just like the ancient Greek story — it looks like a gift (a useful app or file), but hides a threat inside.
examples: Fake antivirus software that is itself malware

glossary.definition: Distributed Denial of Service — an attack that overwhelms a website or service with massive amounts of traffic from many sources, making it unavailable to legitimate users.
glossary.analogy: Like thousands of people calling a restaurant's phone simultaneously — the lines are jammed and real customers can't get through.
examples: Mirai botnet attack taking down major DNS providers (2016)
Online gaming services taken offline during peak hours

glossary.definition: The process of regularly applying updates and security fixes (patches) to software and operating systems to close known vulnerabilities.
glossary.analogy: Like fixing the locks on your house every time a locksmith discovers a new way they could be picked.

glossary.definition: An attack method where an attacker systematically tries every possible combination of passwords or keys until the correct one is found.
glossary.analogy: Like trying every key on a giant keyring until one opens the lock.
examples: Automated tools guessing common passwords against login forms

behavior_nudges: Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) on your email account today — it takes under 2 minutes and dramatically increases your security.
Check if your email has been in a data breach at haveibeenpwned.com — it's free and takes 10 seconds.
Lock your screen every time you walk away from your computer (Win+L on Windows, Control+Command+Q on Mac).
Use a different password for every account — a free password manager like Bitwarden makes this easy.
Before clicking any link, hover over it to see where it actually leads. Does the URL match what you'd expect?
Update your operating system and apps regularly — many attacks exploit known bugs that patches already fix.
Be sceptical of any message that creates urgency or threatens consequences if you don't act immediately.
Never share your OTP (one-time password) with anyone — legitimate companies will never ask for it.
Back up your important files regularly to an external drive or cloud service. This protects you from ransomware.
On public Wi-Fi? Use a VPN or avoid accessing sensitive accounts like banking or email.
Review the permissions your apps have — does that game really need access to your microphone?
Enable automatic updates on your phone — security patches are often bundled in routine updates.
If a deal, offer, or prize sounds too good to be true, it almost certainly is.
Use a strong, unique passphrase for your password manager master password — this is the most important password you have.
Regularly review the devices and apps connected to your Google, Apple, or Microsoft account and remove any you don't recognise.
Set up a recovery email and phone number for your important accounts so you can regain access if locked out.
Be careful what personal information you share on social media — attackers use it to craft convincing phishing messages.
When in doubt, go directly to a company's official website by typing the URL yourself rather than clicking any link.

threat_cards.title: Ransomware
threat_cards.description: Malware that encrypts your files and demands a payment to restore access.
warning_signs: Files you cannot open with unfamiliar extensions (.locked, .encrypted)
prevention: Keep regular offline backups (3-2-1 rule)
Never open unexpected email attachments
Keep software patched and updated
Use reputable antivirus software
if_infected: Disconnect from the internet immediately
Do NOT pay the ransom (no guarantee of recovery)
Report to your local cybercrime authority
Restore from a clean backup

threat_cards.title: Phishing
threat_cards.description: Fraudulent messages designed to trick you into revealing sensitive information or clicking malicious links.
warning_signs: Urgency or threats ('Your account will be closed')
Links that don't match the supposed sender
Requests for passwords, PINs, or payment details
prevention: Check sender email addresses carefully
Hover over links before clicking
Enable spam filters
Use MFA so stolen passwords alone can't compromise accounts
if_infected: Change passwords for any accounts you logged into
Enable MFA immediately
Check bank/credit card statements for unauthorised transactions
Report the phishing email to your provider

threat_cards.title: Malware
threat_cards.description: Any malicious software including viruses, trojans, spyware, and adware designed to harm or compromise your device.
warning_signs: Programs opening or closing on their own
Unknown programs in your app list
prevention: Only download software from official sources
Keep antivirus software up to date
Scan USB drives before opening files
Be cautious with email attachments and downloads
if_infected: Run a full antivirus scan immediately
Disconnect from the internet
Consider a full system restore if infection is severe
Change all passwords from a clean device

threat_cards.title: Social Engineering
threat_cards.description: Psychological manipulation that tricks people into revealing information or performing actions that compromise security.
warning_signs: Pressure to act quickly or secretly
prevention: Verify identities through official channels before acting
Establish a code word with family for emergency calls
Be sceptical of any unsolicited urgent request
Follow your organisation's security procedures even under pressure
if_infected: If you gave information: change passwords and enable MFA
Contact your bank immediately if financial details were shared
Report the incident to relevant authorities
Inform others who may be targeted

threat_cards.title: Identity Theft
threat_cards.description: When someone steals your personal information to impersonate you, typically for financial fraud.
warning_signs: Bills or calls about accounts you didn't open
Rejected credit applications with no explanation
prevention: Shred documents with personal information
Monitor your credit report regularly
Use strong, unique passwords
Enable fraud alerts with your bank
if_infected: Place a fraud alert with credit bureaus
Review all financial statements immediately
File a report with police and relevant authorities
Contact each affected company directly
